raw_response:
Alright, let me think this through as myself — 70 years old, primary school, farming these two mu since I was twenty-some years old.

---

Well, it's two mu. Not much. My wife helps a little when her knees allow, our son works in the city — sends money sometimes, calls on holidays. Government gives me a bit of pension too. So the land isn't really feeding us anymore, but I keep it going. The grain fills our flour jar and I sell the rest. At my age, what would I do without it? Sit in the courtyard all day?

I do things the way I've always done them. Fifty years, I haven't seen much reason to change. The extension fellow came through the village a few years back talking about soil tests and such — I listened politely. Then I did what I always do.

**Wheat first.** After the maize comes off at end of September, I find a neighbor with a small tractor to rotary till — about 60 yuan a mu, done in a morning. I sow around October 10th, maybe a few days later if the soil's too dry. I buy the seed at the shop in town, whatever they're selling that year — Jimai something. About 20 jin per mu, costs maybe 20 yuan a mu. I used to save my own seed but the new varieties you can't really do that, and honestly the shop seed yields better.

For fertilizer on wheat I put down one bag of compound — 复合肥, the 15-15-15 kind — per mu before sowing. That's one 50-jin bag. Then when the wheat greens up in spring and starts jointing, around April, I carry half a bag of urea per mu down the rows and scatter it by hand. If it rains after that's best, washes it in. If the wheat looks pale I might add a bit more but usually it's fine. Two bags compound plus a bag of urea for the whole two mu — that's what I buy.

I irrigate the wheat three times. Winter water late November before the ground freezes hard, then again at green-up in March, and once more when the grain is filling in May. The well is a hundred paces from the plot, I pay the electric — maybe 25 yuan a mu each time. If May has good rain I skip that last one.

Weeds in the wheat I spray once in spring — the shop sells a packet, you mix it with water. 20 yuan a mu or so. Rust some years I see red spots on the leaves, then I ask what to do. Usually nothing serious.

Harvest is June, early-middle. The combine goes through the village, 60 yuan a mu, takes half an hour for my two mu. Good year I get 450 jin a mu, bad year 350. Average maybe 420.

**Then maize, right after.** No time to plow — the wheat stubble is still standing when the maize needs to go in. A fellow comes with a direct seeder, plants into the stubble, 30 yuan a mu. Mid-June, within a week of wheat harvest. Seed is hybrid, whatever variety the neighbors are praising — Zhengdan or Xianyu, usually. Seed costs more than wheat, maybe 35 yuan a mu.

For maize fertilizer same routine — one bag of compound per mu at planting (the seeder drops it with the seed), then half a bag of urea per mu when the maize is knee-high, end of July. I walk it in by hand between the rows.

Maize water — depends on the summer. Usually July and August have thunderstorms enough. If it turns dry around tasseling in August I'll pump once. Maize needs less water than wheat, and my body needs less running around too.

Herbicide once right after planting, before the weeds come up — 20 yuan a mu. That's it for chemicals on maize. Pests are mostly the borer and I don't usually spray for it.

Harvest late September with the combine again, 60 yuan a mu. Good year 500 jin a mu, sometimes a bit more. Then back to wheat.

**What I watch.** I can't do the heavy work anymore — bent over too many years. Every year I pay more to the machine fellows and that eats into what little profit there is. But I can't not farm. Land sits bad when it's empty. As long as my wife and I can walk the field, spread the fertilizer, pay for the combine and the water, we'll keep at it. If the price of urea jumps again like two years back, maybe I'll put on a little less. If the government pays the seed subsidy on time, that helps.
